title: 10 iPhone Accessibility features that are useful for everyone
content:
Macworld


Apple has always been renowned for adapting its systems to meet the needs of people with disabilities. Anyone who selects Accessibility in the Settings app on an iPhone will be overwhelmed by the sheer range of options available. There are settings for short-sighted people like me, and there are settings for people with age-related vision impairment. There are settings for hearing aids, and a voice can read out the screen content.
As is always the case with Apple’s Accessibility features, there are sliders and buttons tucked away in unexpected places that make life a little easier for all users. Here is a collection of our favorite Accessibility features you could be using.


Face ID attention check

				
					

				
			
Foundry




There’s a rather clever option for Face ID: the biometric module only unlocks the iPhone when you’re looking directly at it. This prevents accidental unlocks. The setting is tucked away in Accessibility under Face ID and Attention.
The system warns you about certain types of sunglasses, but in practice, the unlocking works quite reliably. I’ve never had any problems with my polarized sunglasses. Another useful option is haptic feedback upon successful authentication. You’ll receive a brief vibration when Apple Pay is successful or when the iPhone is unlocked using Face ID.






Notifications with a flash

				
					

				
			
Foundry




You can choose to have notifications on your iPhone signaled visually rather than with an audio alert. This uses the LED flash on the rear camera or a flashing display. The setting can be found under Audio and Visual and is called Flash for Alerts. 
Receiving a large number of notifications can drain the battery more quickly, as the flash or screen is actively switched on.






Always show volume controls

				
					

				
			
Foundry




As part of the Liquid Glass design for iOS 26, Apple removed the volume slider from the widgets. The volume itself could still be controlled via dedicated buttons, gestures on the AirPods, or the Digital Crown on the Apple Watch. The only thing missing was an overview of just how loud AC/DC were rocking or how softly Lana Del Rey was whispering.
However, the slider has never actually disappeared; it can be reactivated in Accessibility under the Audio and Visual section.






No Liquid Glass

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The Liquid Glass interface is here to stay. From the next version of iOS onwards, Apple will no longer accept apps that haven’t yet adapted their appearance to Liquid Glass. However, you can at least make the content stand out better against the background using two settings.
These settings can be found in Accessibility under the Display & Text Size section. The first two sliders after the text settings are called Reduce Transparency and Increase Contrast. Together, these create a clear distinction between the foreground and background, making text easier to read.






On/Off Labels

				
					

				
			
Foundry




If you want to bring a bit of that retro look from previous iOS versions to your iPhone, you can also enable additional On/Off labels in the Display & Text Size section. Instead of relying solely on color cues such as grey and green, the system also provides graphical cues such as a vertical line for On and a circle for Off. These are perhaps the last traces of skeuomorphism in iOS, as the line and circle represent the 0 and 1 in binary code.






Make Siri always aware

				
					

				
			
Foundry




By default, Siri is disabled when the iPhone face down or when the screen is covered. You can change this behavior in Accessibility: go to the Siri section at the end of Accessibility, then turn on Always Listen for Siri. This allows you to activate the smart voice assistant regardless of the iPhone’s position.






Tap on the back

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The Back Tap feature has an interesting history. The Accessibility team at Apple faced a problem with the iPhone X: The Home button disappeared entirely, and with it an intuitive and easy way to take screenshots. Pressing the Volume Up and Power buttons simultaneously requires a fair bit of guitar-playing-like skill, but the team wanted a simple yet effective alternative for people with disabilities.
This is how the double-tap gesture on the back of the iPhone came about as a replacement for the Home button. Initially, it could only be used to take screenshots, but now it offers  several tasks that can be assigned to these taps.
The feature can be found in the Accessibility section, under Touch > Back Tap. You can set up a double-tap and a triple-tap. If you turn on Show Banner, a banner will appear when the iPhone senses a double or triple tap.






Background sounds

				
					

				
			
Foundry




ASMR videos on YouTube attract millions of views: the simple sounds of running water, wind or a crackling fire help people to relax or even fall asleep. Your iPhone can play such sounds too (without ad breaks).
The list of all background sounds can be found in Accessibility under the Audio & Visual section. Under the Background Sound > Sound setting, you’ll find a list of several available options, including Ocean, Rain, Babble, Fire, Airplane, and three different types of white noise. The sounds work even without an internet connection, as the iPhone downloads the relevant soundtrack the first time you play it.
The Background Sound page has several different settings you’ll want to adjust, including Volume, Stop Sounds with a Timer, and more. You can use these background sounds to help you fall asleep and set them to stop at a specific time. 






Reduce frame rate to 60 fps

				
					

				
			
Foundry




On compatible iPhones, you can reduce the refresh rate to 60 frames per second. This is particularly beneficial when using graphically intensive apps. This setting can help reduce heat build-up slightly.. The setting can be found in Accessibility under the Motion section. The setting is at the bottom, called Limit Frame Rate.






One-handed mode

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Having one-handed mode enabled is a must, especially on the larger iPhones. With a downward swipe at the bottom of the screen, all content moves down a little further. Those items become easier to reach. This setting is called Reachability, and the toggle can be found in Accessibility under Touch.

title: Apple Plans iPhone-to-Windows Copy and Paste in EU After Microsoft Request
content:
Apple is working on a new feature that will support cross-device copy and paste between iOS devices and Windows PCs.


Microsoft asked for the feature using Apple's EU interoperability request system for developers, which Apple implemented to comply with the Digital Markets Act. Apple began evaluating the request in March, and on June 26, proposed a project plan. 

Microsoft described how the feature would be used:

 	
Copy text or other supported content on their iPhone and paste it directly on their Windows PC, and vice versa.

 	
Perform common productivity workflows without needing to foreground an app or take explicit repeated actions to initiate a transfer.

 	
Experience clipboard synchronization as a lightweight, continuous capability rather than a manual, app-driven operation.


Apple proposed a solution that would let an iPhone share and import items from the pasteboard to a paired accessory, like a Windows PC. Apple plans to use a solution similar to the Accessory Notifications option it added for third-party wearables in the EU in iOS 26.5. Users would need to give a paired device one-time permission to paste content from an iPhone.
To adopt this solution, you will need to adopt AccessorySetupKit in order for the user to consent to the necessary permissions allowing the pasteboard to be shared with your accessory. This solution will require the user to perform a one-time consent to sharing the pasteboard with each paired accessory that will receive this functionality.

Right now, an app can only read an iPhone's clipboard if the app is actively running in the foreground and the user grants clipboard access with each copy/paste action. For its own devices, Apple has a Universal Clipboard feature with cross-device copy and paste between iOS and macOS.

Microsoft complained that the clipboard restrictions imposed on apps prevent the continuous synchronization of clipboard content from an iPhone to a PC or other connected device in the background. 

Apple says introducing cross-device copy and paste is a significant engineering effort, with work expected to be complete by fall 2027. It will be shipped first in a developer beta for testing ahead of a public release. If the feature is added toward the end of fall 2027, it could be early 2028 before the public gets access.

It is likely that cross-device copy and paste will be limited to iPhone and Windows users in the European Union, though it is possible Apple could implement it worldwide. 

brought some features it was required to support under the DMA to all countries, like eSIM transfers from iPhone to Android and simpler data transfers when switching between Android devices and iPhones. Other features, like AirPods-style pairing and notification forwarding for third-party wearables, have only rolled out in the EU.

title: Report: Apple aiming to launch camera-equipped AirPods this fall
content:
Macworld


We’ve been reporting on Apple’s plan to stick cameras on AirPods Pro since summer 2024, believe it or not. It was supposed to happen earlier, but setbacks in Apple Intelligence and Siri delayed them, just like Siri delayed Apple’s new HomePod mini and its push into the smart home market.
Now, according to a brief update in Mark Gurman’s Power On newsletter at Bloomberg, they could finally be on the way this fall alongside Apple’s other smart home products.
Gurman says the original camera-equipped AirPods were developed under the codename B798. Apple frequently develops multiple competing versions of the same product, and in this case, one of the alternative designs was codenamed B790. This B790 version, Gurman reports, appears to be further along, with the code name already referenced in the OS 27 betas and a scheduled launch as early as this fall, barring any further delays.
What are camera-equipped AirPods?
The AirPods-with-cameras have been rumored long enough that we sort of expected them to be the AirPods Pro 3. We got a heart rate sensor instead, along with some battery life and audio improvements.
Supposedly, the AirPods with cameras are said to resemble AirPods Pro 3, and it’s not yet known if they will include a heart rate sensor or not. It’s also not known what the name will be: AirPods Pro 4, AirPods Ultra, or something else entirely.
The cameras are said to see both standard spectrum and infrared, but reportedly won’t be used for taking photos and videos—the quality and placement would be poor for that. Instead, the cameras are meant to be used for AI-powered features. That could be recognizing your hands for gesture controls, adjusting audio based on the environment, or recognizing if someone is talking to you or just talking nearby. It could also be used to give Siri a set of “eyes” where the AI assistant can give you answers that are appropriate for the context of your current surroundings and activity as part of Visual Intelligence.
There are lots of other possibilities for AirPods with cameras that would necessitate changes to other Apple software and services, too. Think of workout tracking that can count reps and sets when you lift weights, or nutrition tracking based on ingredient labels or analyzing what’s on your plate. Currently, there’s no information to suggest any specific use case for the camera-equipped AirPods, but there are lots of possibilities, now and in the future.

title: Apple's iCloud File Sharing Left Ex-Employees With Access to Secret Documents
content:
The way Apple combines work and personal iCloud accounts left some employees able to access confidential documents after departing the company, reports The Information. The site spoke to more than half a dozen former Apple employees who were unknowingly left with access to sensitive content.


The former employees said many Apple files they had been shared on over their careers at the company—including planning documents for product launch events—continued to sync to their personal devices through the iCloud storage service after they left Apple. In some cases, they even received notifications about fresh updates to the documents. Some former employees said they were petrified to delete the files for fear that doing so would attract Apple's attention.

Apple files get mixed in with employees' accounts because the company encourages them to use their personal Apple Accounts with their work ‌iCloud‌ account. Employees are given a 2TB ‌iCloud‌ plan and are able to merge the storage with their existing Apple Account or create a new account. Since only one primary account can be signed in at a time, most opt to use their existing account to avoid having to carry two iPhones.

Apple has a managed folder for workplace files that it revokes access to when an employee leaves, but some internal documents aren't saved there automatically and shared files end up mixed in with personal content. Employees can also retain access to iMessage chats and files shared via the Messages app.

In its filing, Apple alleged that former employee Chang Liu breached Apple's systems using a "rare, previously unknown authentication bug" to download files while he was working at OpenAI.

The Information that the OpenAI lawsuit is unrelated to any files left available on ‌iCloud‌ and that it does not pursue legal claims against former employees who accidentally have Apple documents in their personal ‌iCloud‌ accounts.
This case is about OpenAI employees wrongfully taking Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products. Nothing in the filing relates to documents shared by, or stored in, iCloud.

Former employees say Apple does not do a thorough enough job going through personal devices to remove sensitive files that have been stored in ‌iCloud‌. In a now-settled legal dispute, chip company Rivos claimed Apple intentionally lets former employees retain access to files "as part of a planned effort to generate a pretextual basis to sue the employees and their new employer for 'stealing' Apple material." In the Rivos case, an employee was targeted for keeping work files in his personal ‌iCloud‌ account.

Another former Apple employee sued by Apple, Gerard Williams, countersued and accused the company of using intimidation tactics to scare people thinking of leaving. Apple sued Williams for breach of contract after he started processor company Nuvia, presenting extensive phone and text records of his communications. The court rejected Williams' claim, and Apple dropped the case in 2023.

also accused former Vision Pro engineer Di Liu of downloading thousands of corporate documents to his personal cloud storage shortly before leaving the company for Snap.

The Information does not outright suggest Apple is purposefully allowing former employees to retain access to ‌iCloud‌ files, but points out that Apple's use of ‌iCloud‌ for file sharing and its incomplete wiping of employee accounts are at odds with its heavy focus on privacy and security.

title: If you want a MacBook Air, you should buy one ASAP
content:
Macworld


First it was the Mac mini. Then the Mac Studio. Now, the memory crisis is aiming to wipe out stock of yet another Mac, this one far more popular.
If you’re looking to buy a MacBook Air, it might be hard to find one before the end of August. As we saw with the Mac mini earlier this year, delivery estimates on Apple.com are beginning to show delays as Apple scrambles to get more stock.
As reported by Mark Gurman in his latest Power On newsletter, the seemingly minor delay on Apple.com—orders are currently shipping with a two-week backlog—is indicative of a much larger issue caused by memory shortages. Gurman reports that Apple is scrambling to keep new MacBooks in stock during the back-to-school and upcoming holiday shopping seasons by sourcing RAM from China and “prominently steering customers toward the base MacBook Pro,” which starts at $1,999, several hundred dollars more than the $1,299 Air.
Upselling is a tactic Apple rarely deploys at its stores, and it could backfire. Apple has built a ton of trust with consumers over the years by largely letting buyers dictate the budget they want to spend, whether that means an iPad, iMac, or MacBook. Coupled with price hikes that are still fresh in people’s minds, steering consumers into higher-end products they don’t need could cross the line from sensible to sleazy.
Apple isn’t expected to update the MacBook Air with an M6 processor until spring 2027, though it’s unclear whether that will fix the issue. The M6 MacBook Air is expected to use the same LPDDR5X RAM as the current model, and there are no signs that the supply issues will ease before 2028. In its recent financial results conference call, Tim Cook reiterated that Apple is facing “a hundred-year flood on the memory pricing” and is “evaluating all options” to balance costs and supply.
On Monday morning, Amazon still had the 13-inch MacBook Air in stock for $1,243, about $50 less than the Apple Store, which was quoting an August 18-25 delivery window. Also reader David points out that Apple’s refurbished store has several in stock as well for $200 less than you’d pay for a new one. Apple refurbs come with a full 1-year warranty and go through a “rigorous” inspection process.
But whichever model you choose, you should probably act fast.

title: Best Games for Mac 2026: A-list Mac games to play
content:
Macworld


For years, gaming on a Mac meant compromises: fewer releases, weaker performance, and the quiet assumption that serious players needed a Windows PC. That’s no longer entirely true.
Thanks to Apple silicon, improved developer support, and a growing number of high-quality ports, there are now genuinely great games that run well on macOS. Not just indie experiments or casual time-killers, but full-scale RPGs, strategy games, and visually demanding titles that take advantage of modern Mac hardware.
This list focuses on the best Mac games you can play right now, not everything that technically runs on macOS. Every game here was chosen based on performance on Apple silicon, quality of the Mac version, and whether it’s actually worth your time and money. We’ve also excluded games that rely heavily on emulation or feel meaningfully worse than their Windows counterparts.
Mac gaming still isn’t perfect, but if you own a recent Mac, it’s better than it’s ever been. These are the games that prove it. 
Best Mac Games to play in 2026
There are so many great games available to play on the Mac. Everyone has different tastes though, so we’ve tried to include something for everyone below. So whether you love RPGs, fighting games, action-adventure, first-person shooters, strategy games or puzzle, read on to find something to play.
Below you can find the best games released in 2025, plus the ones we loved and will continue to play in 2026. Updated August 2026 to add our reviews of Total War: Attila and Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition.

More than 25 years after the original game first appeared on Mac, Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition has finally arrived as a native macOS release thanks to Feral Interactive. While it has taken an extraordinarily long time to get here, the wait has been worthwhile. This remastered version updates one of the greatest real-time strategy (RTS) games ever made with sharper high-resolution graphics, bundled expansion content and Apple Silicon support, making it feel at home on modern Macs.
The game spans roughly a thousand years of history, from the Dark Ages through the Medieval era, allowing players to command dozens of civilizations in campaigns inspired by real historical figures such as Joan of Arc, Attila the Hun and Vlad Dracula. The Definitive Edition includes the original game alongside three DLC expansions, dramatically increasing the amount of content with additional civilizations, maps and historical campaigns. Combined with skirmishes and replayable scenarios, there are hundreds of hours of strategy gameplay available.
Gameplay remains as compelling as ever. Players must gather resources, expand settlements, research technologies and build armies while responding to enemy attacks in real time. Although experienced strategy fans will quickly feel at home, the game also includes excellent tutorials that teach both basic mechanics and more advanced tactical concepts, making it approachable for newcomers.
The Mac version does have a few drawbacks. It only supports Apple Silicon Macs, leaving older Intel machines behind. Multiplayer is also restricted to Mac users, so there is no cross-platform play with Windows players. In addition, the interface occasionally shows its age, and the game does a poor job of explaining that the enhanced graphics pack requires a separate free download after installation.
Fortunately, these issues do little to diminish what is still one of the finest RTS games ever created. The updated visuals preserve the charm of the original while making battles look crisp on modern displays, and the sheer volume of campaigns and historical scenarios provides outstanding value for money.
For Mac owners who enjoy strategy games, Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition is an easy recommendation. It successfully modernises a timeless classic without losing the gameplay that made it legendary, proving that great strategy games never go out of style.

Total War: Attila was originally launched for Intel Macs and PCs way back in 2015 – when the macOS was still called OS X. Needless to say, changes to both Apple’s hardware and operating systems meant that the Mac version fell by the wayside several years ago, but Feral Interactive has now brought the game back to the Mac, providing native support for current Apple Silicon Macs, and Apple’s Metal graphics system (although it no longer runs on Intel Macs anymore, unfortunately). At the moment, the game is currently only available on Steam – and requires macOS 15.7 or later to run – although Feral tells us that it will be released on the Mac App Store later this year.
 Following on from last year’s Total War: Rome, the action this time around moves forward to 370AD as the now faltering Roman Empire has split into two rival factions and finds itself under attack on all fronts. There’s a prologue section that begins with the Battle Of Olbia, which acts as a tutorial for new players as well as setting the historical context for the campaign ahead of you. When you’re ready, you can begin the main campaign by taking control of any of the various factions within the game. You can command the Eastern Roman Empire, the Saxons of the Barbarian Kingdoms, or the Sassanids of the Persian Eastern Empire. But, of course, the star of the show is Jason Momoa – aka the beardy warlord Attila, who leads the fearsome hordes of the Hun.
 In previous Total War games you had to build up your forces by methodically gathering resources, such as wood, stone and gold, which then allowed you to train your troops and develop new weapons. However, the Hun tribes are nomadic, so instead of settling in a specific region and quietly developing towns and cities, the Huns charge across Europe on horseback, raiding the lands of their enemies to gain wealth and resources. This makes for a more dynamic playing style where you can throw caution to the winds and unleash the Huns to swarm across Europe, wreaking havoc left, right and center. You can hit the ground running and start raiding and pillaging right from the start of the campaign, giving Total War: Attila a more ‘invade first, ask questions later’ style of play than other games in the series.
 The age of the game also means that you don’t need a high-end Mac to run it properly. We had no problems running it on a MacBook Pro with an M2 processor, and the game’s graphics settings provide presets that are suitable for a wide range of Mac models. Once the main campaign is complete you can buy a number of expansion packs that extend the campaign further, or test yourself by recreating a number of great historical battles or setting up your own custom battles against computer-controlled opponents. There’s an online multiplayer mode as well although – as with many Mac games – you are limited to playing only with other Mac players.

Slay the Spire 2 is a confident sequel that builds on one of the most successful deck-building games available on Mac. Rather than dramatically changing the formula, developer Mega Crit focuses on refining what made the original so addictive, introducing a host of small improvements, more content and a new cooperative multiplayer mode. The result is a game that feels familiar but remains fresh enough to justify the sequel.
The core gameplay remains unchanged. Players battle their way up a mysterious spire by choosing different routes through a map of rooms, fighting monsters, collecting new cards and relics, and making strategic decisions about how to strengthen their deck. As a roguelike, every defeat sends you back to the beginning, encouraging experimentation and rewarding players who learn how different cards and abilities work together. The game remains easy to pick up but offers plenty of depth for players willing to master its systems.
While the sequel doesn’t reinvent the experience, it adds considerably more variety. Returning characters are joined by two new classes, the Necrobinder and the Regent, each bringing fresh abilities and play styles. There are more skills, relics and rare cards to discover, along with new quests and encounters that encourage players to rethink their route through each run. Daily challenges and custom game modes also return, while the headline new feature is a co-op mode for up to four players, allowing friends to tackle the Spire together for the first time.
Our main criticism is the presentation. Although the 2D graphics have been improved, the visuals remain fairly basic, lacking the atmosphere and visual flair found in some rival games. However, those simple graphics also help the game run smoothly on both Intel and Apple Silicon Macs, making it accessible to a wide range of hardware.
Overall, Slay the Spire 2 is an excellent sequel. It may not introduce many major new ideas, but its numerous refinements, additional content and enjoyable co-op mode make it a must-have for fans of the original. Newcomers, however, may want to start with the first game before moving on to the sequel.

Why we loved Blue Prince: Blue Prince is one of the most inventive puzzle-adventure games in years, blending roguelike mechanics with atmospheric mystery in a way that feels both fresh and deeply satisfying. Its constantly shifting mansion keeps you thinking strategically and creatively, while its layered secrets reward curiosity. 
Blue Prince is an indie puzzle-adventure that updates the feel of classic exploration games with slick 3D visuals and a mystery-driven structure that’s perfect for Mac players. In the game you’re Simon P. Jones, heir to the mysterious Mt. Holly mansion, and your only path to inheriting the estate is to locate the elusive “Room 46.” To do that you explore a sprawling 45-room mansion where the layout changes every in-game day, forcing you to rethink your approach constantly.
As you wander from room to room, you choose which spaces to open next, building out your blueprint while managing a limited number of steps. Some rooms contain useful items that grant extra movement, while others offer clues tied to deeper mysteries hidden in the mansion. Because the mansion resets each night, planning ahead and taking careful notes becomes a strategic part of the experience, giving the game the feel of a mystery you’re slowly unraveling over many sessions.
Visually, Blue Prince blends hand-drawn charm with true 3D exploration, creating a warm but curious atmosphere that suits its puzzle focus. The pacing is unhurried; it favors thoughtful investigation over action, so it’s well suited to fans of cerebral, methodical games rather than fast-paced thrills.
Overall, Blue Prince will likely appeal most to players who enjoy deep mystery, clever puzzles, and the satisfaction of piece-by-piece discovery. Its blend of adventure, strategy, and roguelike resets makes it an engaging experience for curious players on macOS.

Why we loved Cyberpunk 2077: Cyberpunk 2077 (Ultimate Edition) nailed the comeback. The vast, neon-soaked world of Night City offers deep freedom, compelling characters and quests, and slick futuristic visuals. After many patches (and expansion Phantom Liberty), it plays smoothly even on Macs – making the once-troubled RPG feel “alive” and worth exploring.
Cyberpunk 2077, despite its troubled 2020 launch, sold more than 30 million copies. Now CD Projekt Red has made Cyberpunk: 2077 available for the Mac—on the App Store, Steam, and Epic Games Store.
The game is set in the Blade Runner-inspired Night City, a megalopolis obsessed with power, glamour, and body modification. 
Initially, the first-person viewpoint suggests a straightforward FPS, but it’s actually a deep and challenging role-playing game that boldly steps into the future, avoiding tired fantasy clichés. 
Your character – who can be male or female – is a hacker known as V, and you start the game by choosing one of three ‘lifepaths’ that fill in V’s background. You can assign experience points to attributes such as intelligence, reflexes, technical ability and ‘cool’, with each attribute giving you access to different skills that you can develop throughout the game. And, of course, there are plenty of body modifications and upgrades that you can collect along the way too. 
V is sent on a mission to steal a prototype chip called the Relic, but then ends up with the Relic implanted inside their own head. It turns out that the chip stores the digital personality of a dead anti-corporate rockstar called Johnny Silverhand (played by Keanu Reeves). Johnny soon starts to take over, forcing you to find a way to save your own personality before it is overwritten.
Night City provides a huge open world that you can explore. There’s a varied cast of characters that you can meet and plenty of jobs that you can pick up. There are few games on the Mac that create the same sense of freedom – you can spend hours exploring before tackling the main quest. 
The action can get pretty violent, and there’s lots of bad language too, so it isn’t for younger gamers.
The team at CD Projekt Red say that it will run on Macs with a basic M1 processor – but you’ll need macOS 15.5 and at least 16GB of memory (there’s no support for Intel Macs). There are presets that adjust graphics settings for different Mac models to get the best performance from the game.

Why we loved Assassin’s Creed, Shadows: Assassin’s Creed Shadows impressed us because it delivers a richly realized feudal-Japan setting, blending ninja-style stealth and samurai combat with satisfying variety and depth. Players can switch between two contrasting protagonists – a stealthy shinobi and a powerful samurai – giving the game flexibility and replay value. The open world and generous quests add to the sense of immersion and adventure.
Shadows is the first game in the long-running Assassin’s Creed series that has been released on the Mac. It’s set in Japan during a civil war in 1579 as the warlord Oda Nobunaga attempts to conquer and forcibly unite the country’s warring factions. 
You to play as two separate characters, each with their own different skills and fighting styles. Naoe is a shinobi (ninja) who specialises in stealth and agility. Yasuke, a samurai who can block and parry his foes’ attacks. It’s pretty violent but you can tone down the settings for blood and dismemberment if you want. This one isn’t for kids. 
The game does take a little while to get going, as it effectively has two introductions to allow you to get some practice with the different fighting styles of Naoe and Yasuke. Things soon pick up, though.  
Shadows provides plenty of quests and combat to keep you busy. For the most part, it’s all about the wall-to-wall combat, with lots of sneaking and parkour-style running and jumping to add variety. There are four difficulty settings available – which will be helpful for Mac users who haven’t played any of the Assassin’s Creed games before. 
What most impressed me were the game’s 3D graphics. The early cut-scenes were very impressive, with some of the most detailed and photo-realistic effects that I’ve ever seen on a Mac. With many games, though, and when the cut-scenes finish you find that the actual in-game action tends to offer a lower level of visual detail, but, with Shadows, the game just continues smoothly at the end of these cut-scenes and maintains the excellent visual quality throughout the game.

Why we loved Hollow Knight, Silksong: Hollow Knight: Silksong won us over with its gorgeous hand-drawn art, fluid combat, and atmospheric world that runs smoothly even on modest Macs. It brings back the tight platform-action and exploration that made its predecessor a cult classic – but sharper and more ambitious.
The game feels like a polished, meaningful evolution: faster and more agile hero, deeper environments, memorable bosses — a worthy sequel that still respects the original vibe.
Silksong works on both Intel Macs and Apple Silicon. The game’s 2D graphics run smoothly on older Macs, including my five-year-old Intel iMac at 4K resolution. 
Hollow Knight, developed by a modest three-man team in Adelaide, was a huge hit and sold millions of copies. The sequel has built up significant anticipation, but Team Cherry took their time to ensure Silksong lived up to its award-winning predecessor.
Silksong follows Hornet, a princess from the last game, as she escapes from a new kingdom called Pharloom. Despite sharing the same distinctive hand-drawn graphics, animation, and Larkin’s soundtrack, the game introduces new mechanics. Hornet navigates a sideways-scrolling 2D platform game, using her needle and thread weapons to defeat over 200 enemies. As she explores Pharloom, she gains new weapons and abilities to tackle the game’s bosses.
While I’m not skilled at platform games, I found the jumping mechanics in Silksong more forgiving than in Hollow Knight. Sometimes, Hornet could grab a ledge and escape danger if I missed a jump.
That said, Silkong is more challenging than its predecessors, with varied movement and powerful bosses.
Silksong’s opening screen suggests using a game controller, which I prefer with a keyboard and mouse. However, I struggled to adjust the keyboard controls to make Hornet move quickly. The Save system is also frustrating, only allowing saves at specific points like benches, forcing repeated retracing of steps to overcome obstacles or enemies.
While platform games can be frustrating, especially with restrictive Save systems, Silksong stands out for those who enjoy them. It’s one of the few games on the Mac that matches its challenge and style, making it a worthy successor to Hollow Knight.  
Silksong costs $19.99/£16.75 on Steam and Gog, and buying it once grants access to both PC and Mac versions. The first game is also on sale, making it an affordable introduction to the series.

Why we loved Control, Ultimate Edition: Control nails a creepy, surreal vibe. Its moody, inter-dimensional setting and uncanny architecture draw you in immediately. Combat mixes gunplay with psychic powers, letting you telekinetically fling debris or use a shape-shifting “Service Weapon,” keeping fights fresh and flexible. It’s also impressive technically: runs well on modern Macs (M1 or later), meaning you get immersive visuals and smooth performance without needing beefy hardware.
Control, a unique super-powered shoot-‘em-up action game with X-Files-inspired vibes, took a while to reach the Mac. It was worth the wait.
The game begins with Jesse Faden arriving at the headquarters of the Federal Bureau of Control (FBC), a government agency investigating paranormal ‘Altered World Events’ (AWEs). Jesse’s younger brother vanished during an AWE, and she’s guided by a mysterious voice to the FBC.
The FBC office, known as the Oldest House, is eerily quiet when Jesse arrives, with only a creepy janitor providing directions to the Director’s office. This opening section serves as a tutorial, introducing the main controls and setting the story. Jesse engages in dialogue with her inner voice as she explores the FBC.
Upon finding the Director’s office, she discovers he’s dead, having killed himself with his hand gun. This ordinary gun, the Service Weapon, whispers instructions to Jesse, recruiting her into the FBC and assigning missions.
Jesse’s first mission reveals the Oldest House’s connection to another dimension, where she encounters alien figures and experiences combat. The Service Weapon can magically reload, which is helpful since Jesse struggles with shoot-em-up games. She also discovers she has psychic powers, starting with a psychokinetic punch that knocks back enemies. This complements her shooting skills, allowing her to approach enemies and defeat them before shooting. As the game progresses, Jesse enhances her psychokinetic powers, learning to hurl objects and upgrading weapons.
The game does have some flaws. The auto-save feature is irritating, as it only saves at specific points, forcing players to replay sections repeatedly. 
Control requires an M1 processor or later running Sonoma or later, it’s playable on a MacBook Pro with an M2 Pro at 34 frames per second with Medium graphics settings at 2560×1440 resolution. Lowering the resolution and graphics settings can improve performance even with an M1.
The game’s combination of shooter action and psychic powers ensures fun and varied combat, even for those with limited shooting skills. It’s a good choice for those who enjoy challenging and atmospheric action games.

Why we loved Resident Evil 3: Because Resident Evil 3 on Mac delivers solid, classic survival-horror fun — the zombie-slaying remains tense, and the inclusion of Nemesis as a relentless pursuer shakes up the usual formula. The game runs smoothly even on modest Macs (M1 or newer), making it accessible without high-end hardware. It’s a good (and affordable) entry point for newcomers to the series, with a free demo letting you try before you buy.
Capcom is putting in a lot of effort to release Mac versions of its games, especially the Resident Evil series, and as of spring 2025 it’s added a Mac version of Resident Evil 3, a remake of the original game from 1999.
You play as Jill Valentine, a special agent sent to Racoon City to investigate the outbreak of the ‘zombie virus’ that first appeared in Resident Evil 2. Jill and her fellow agents suspect Umbrella, a pharmaceutical corporation that developed the T-Virus, the biological weapon behind the outbreak. In most Resident Evil games, you fight zombies, but Resident Evil 3 introduces Nemesis, an intelligent super-zombie that is hunting you down. 
As the hunted instead of the hunter, instead of blasting zombies, you’re on the defensive, constantly pursued by Nemesis as you escape Racoon City. This offers a welcome respite from the usual offensive gameplay in the franchise.
The game doesn’t require a high-end Mac to handle its 3D graphics, but it only runs on Macs with Apple Silicon, not Intel. So that’s an M1 processor or later and macOS 13.0 or later. We tested it on a MacBook Pro with an M2 Pro chip and it ran smoothly, even with hordes of zombies. You can download a demo to see how it runs on your Mac before buying the full version. 
The Mac version also runs on iPhone 15 or later and iPads with an A17 or M-series processor, so you can play it on your mobile devices too.
The Mac version of Resident Evil 3 is currently only available on the Mac App Store.

Why we loved Civilization VII: Civilization VII impressed us because it refreshes the classic strategy formula with bold new ideas – letting you mix-and-match leaders and civilizations, and splitting history into three manageable Ages (Antiquity, Exploration, Modern). Its detailed 3D visuals run smoothly on modern Macs, making empire-building both beautiful and accessible. 
There are changes to the latest game in the long-running Civilization series that are a good way of making the game more accessible for newcomers, though veteran Civ players may feel the new approach is dumbing the game down somewhat.
As usual, you choose a leader and a civilization that you control and develop throughout the ages and your aim is either conquering rival civilizations, or emerging as a world leader through economic, scientific or cultural dominance. But, in Civilization 7, your leader and your society are entirely separate, so you can mix-and-match leaders and countries in historically inaccurate ways. We had Catherine The Great Of Russia leading the armies of ancient Rome rather than 18th century Russia. 
Once you’ve chosen your leader and their civilization you start in any of three different Ages – Antiquity, Exploration, or the Modern Age. You follow four different ‘paths’ that lead to success – economic, cultural, scientific, or military. Focus on one path or diversify and explore the benefits of each. Your leader remains the same as you progress through all three ages, but you get to choose a new civilization each time. 
Dividing the game into ages like this does make it more approachable, as it splits the game into manageable sections. However, some players may miss the military and political intrigue of previous games. 
One criticism that has emerged loud and clear across the board is that the game’s user interface is poorly designed, with unhelpful menus and tool-tips that make it difficult to find the information you need. We found it annoying that the game was constantly badgering us to create an online account in order to use the online multiplayer mode and unlock other bonuses. The developers have announced that they’re working on fine-tuning the interface in response.
Civilization 7 runs natively on Apple Silicon – but not on Intel Macs. It lists Sequoia as the minimum required version of macOS, although we ran it in Sonoma without issue. Performance is good, despite the game’s detailed 3D graphics. The game has a built-in benchmarking tool, and my MacBook’s M2 Pro chip was able to cruise along at a comfortable 55fps using High graphics settings when set at 2,560×1,440 resolution.

Why we loved Hades II: Hades II impressed us because it delivers addictive, fast-paced roguelike action powered by tight combat, a huge variety of weapons/boons, and beautiful art, sound and world design. It’s a worthy follow-up to the original, with deeper mythological storytelling and endlessly replayable runs – making each descent into the underworld feel fresh and rewarding.
Hades II (Early Access) was released for Windows PCs in 2024, but at the end of 2024 an update added native support for Macs with Apple Silicon.
You play Zagreus’ (from the first game) sister, Melinoë, a sorceress with powerful magical abilities who attempts to find and defeat Chronos, the ancient god who was father of Hades and is now waging war on Olympus itself. 
Like Hades, Hades 2 is a ‘roguelike’ game. Roguelike games don’t allow you save the game and reload when you die, so each death means that you have to start again. That can be frustrating, but you can find new weapons and learn new skills as you progress, as well as earning ‘boons’ from the gods that make you more powerful. You also get to keep your skills and upgrades even after you die, so each time you start again you’re a little bit more powerful. There’s a God Mode that gives you a power boost right from the start.
Hades 2 is in Early Access – and looks likely to remain that way for most of 2025 – but it’s pretty solid and stable. The hand-drawn graphics style looks great and the relatively simple 2D shaded graphics mean that you don’t need a particularly powerful Mac to run it (I was able to get 60fps using High graphics settings, even at 4K resolution using a MacBook Pro with M2 processor).
Roguelike games don’t suit everyone, but Hades 2 is a lot of fun and a worthy successor to the original Hades, and it’ll be nice treat for anyone that enjoys challenging arcade action.

Why we like Resident Evil 7, Biohazard: It brings atmospheric, first-person horror to Apple devices with impressive performance on M-series Macs, iPads, and even iPhone. Its low price and free demo make it easy to try, while the eerie found-footage storytelling, tense exploration, and Ethan Winters’ unsettling search through a swampy Louisiana mansion create a deeply immersive, terrifying experience that feels fresh for the series.

Why we like Death Stranding: We like Death Stranding because it delivers a strikingly original, atmospheric experience unlike any other game on the Mac. Its cinematic world, haunting landscapes, and star-studded storytelling create a powerful sense of scale and mystery. Even though much of the gameplay centers on traversal, the challenge of navigating rugged terrain is surprisingly satisfying. Strong performance on Apple Silicon also shows real promise for future Mac gaming
Death Stranding, the idiosyncratic and sometimes downright bizarre game from Hideo Kojima, the renowned developer behind the long-running Metal Gear series, arrived on the Mac in 2024.
The game is set in a near-future version of the United States, in the aftermath of a mysterious apocalyptic event known as the Death Stranding, which has caused the collapse of society. All that’s left are a few scattered communities, which rely on ‘porters’ to deliver supplies and help set up a communications system called the Chiral network. That’s where you come in, playing Sam ‘Porter’ Bridges – who is voiced by, and modeled on the actor Norman Reedus of Walking Dead fame – as he trudges across the country delivering his supplies. Along the way, you’ll encounter terrorists and creepy invisible monsters called BTs (‘beached things’), but your real foe for much of the game is simply the environment around you.
There is some combat in Death Stranding, but your main task as a porter is to struggle across the rocky, ruinous countryside as you embark on a series of missions to deliver your cargo of medicines and other supplies. The game is sometimes described as a ‘walking simulator ’ as you spend much of your time clambering over rocks, up hills, or wading across rushing rivers and streams. That may not sound terribly exciting, but there’s a lot of satisfaction as you struggle to slowly inch your way towards the peak of a craggy hill with your cargo intact.
The game also has a dramatic cinematic flair – possibly a little too cinematic, as the first 45 minutes or so is really just a series of very long cut-scenes, interspersed only by a few brief sequences where you learn how to control Sam as he walks, jumps and wades across the rocky terrain. The long cut-scenes can try your patience in the early stages of the game, but they do look terrific – the landscapes have a cinematic scope, and the 3D graphics are tremendously detailed and realistic. And the feeling that this is the gaming equivalent of a blockbuster Hollywood production is further emphasized by cameos from a number of other Hollywood big names, including Mads Mikkelsen, Guillermo Del Toro, and Lindsay Wagner.
The graphics do require a bit of horsepower though. The game will only run on Macs and iPads that have an Apple Silicon processor (M1 or later), and running macOS 13.3 or iPadOS 17.0. We were pleased to find that the game ran well even on an iMac with an M1 processor, although we did have to lower the resolution to 1920×1080. You might need an M2 or M3 to really enjoy the game’s sweeping vistas and eerie special effects, but seeing a game like Death Stranding running on an M1 iMac gives us some hope for the future of games on the Mac.

Dredge was first released for Windows PCs back in 2023, but the developers at Black Salt Games have launched a Mac version, along with mobile versions for iOS and Android. At first glance, Dredge looks like a quiet, cosy game where you spend your daylight hours calmly fishing the seas around the island of Greater Marrow, occasionally delivering items to people on neighbouring islands, and trying to drum up enough cash to upgrade your fishing boat and equipment. The game’s simple shaded graphics remind me of Monument Valley, and its soothing soundtrack – complete with the sound of lapping waves – almost makes you drift off to sleep.
But you soon detect hints of something strange lurking beneath the surface. A few days of fishing and delivering parcels helps ease you into the game, and then you’re approached by a mysterious figure called the Collector, who asks you to find a number of items that were lost in shipwrecks around the islands. 
This can be a challenge as you need quick reflexes to control the tension in your fishing gear and bring these items to the surface (and a game controller might be a better option here than using a keyboard). It takes time too, and I soon found myself hurrying back to Greater Marrow in the dark one night, only to be attacked by a great undersea creature that wrecked my boat and returned me to my last saved game. 
Things just get creepier from there as you start to uncover the mystery behind all these lost ships, and the full game will keep you busy for 10-12 hours, depending on how much time you spend fishing, treasure-hunting and completing side quests. Admittedly, the excitement in Dredge is doled out sparingly, so it’s not a game for action fans, but the balance between the calm daylight hours and the menace that lurks in the dark creates an oddly soothing rhythm that will appeal to fans of more peaceful gaming pursuits (one review on Steam called it “Animal Crossing meets Lovecraft”).

World Of Warcraft has dominated the MMO genre for almost two decades now, and is one of the few A-list games to have staunchly supported the Mac throughout its history – in fact, it even provided an update that allowed the game to run on Apple Silicon Macs as early as November 2020. It’s had a few ups and downs in recent years – both in the real-world and in the game’s virtual world of Azeroth – but the release of the Dragonflight expansion at the end of 2022 was a welcome return to form, providing some important new features and also updating some of the more dated aspects of the game.
Dragonflight costs $49.99/£39.99, and is required in order to enjoy new features such as raising your characters to the new maximum of Level 70. It also gives you access to the Dragon Isles, which contain four major new zones for you to explore and go adventuring. The Dragon Isles are also home to a new playable race of ‘draconic humanoids’ called Dracthyrs, who can play as the new Evoker class, which has the ability to choose between either healing or combat abilities.
And, on entering the Dragon Isles, you can also obtain your own ‘drake’ – a flying dragon that allows you to learn a new set of ‘dragonriding’ skills that let you fly further, faster and higher as you explore the new zones. Throw in a more streamlined skill tree and a number of improvements to WoW’s aging interface, and the entire game feels more sprightly than it has done for several years. You don’t have to buy Dragonflight straight away though, as WoW still provides a free trial that takes you up to Level 20 for free, while owners of previous versions of the game can still continue to play – without the new Dragonflight features – by paying for a monthly subscription ($12.99/£9.99 per month, with discounts for three-month or six-month subscriptions).

Apple is trying very hard to encourage games developers to come back to the Mac, but – around 30 years ago – there was a time when big-names such as Bungie actually developed their games on the Mac first (until Bungie was taken over by Microsoft).
Before Bungie hit the big time with Halo, it made a name for itself with the Marathon series. The original Marathon games stopped running on the Mac long ago, but the entire Marathon series was recently revived with the help of an open-source programming team called Aleph One. The first Marathon game is now available on Steam as a free download – now called Classic Marathon – and it runs on both Intel and Apple Silicon Macs.
The game is a real blast of retro fun, set aboard a space ship called The Marathon, which has been boarded by alien invaders. Your task is pretty straightforward and mostly involves running along lots of corridors blasting the living daylights out of the aliens. Along the way, you can log in to computer terminals that provide access to the ship’s onboard AI, which points you toward your next target or sends you looking for useful information. There’s a plot twist, though, as there seem to be rival AIs at work, each with their own agenda, and this keeps you thinking about what comes next, as well as just exercising your trigger finger in combat.
The game’s old-school graphics obviously look a bit dated these days, but they have a lot of charm, and there’s a sense of satisfaction as you carefully attempt to pick off your enemies without wasting too much ammo – and a real sense of relief when you come across some spare ammo packs lying on the ground too.
The somewhat clumsy control system isn’t quite so charming – it took me some time reading around on the Internet to discover that there’s no Save Game command, so you just have to hope you can survive all the way to the next checkpoint, where your game is saved automatically. But that’s part of the fun, as it puts extra pressure on you to stay alive, and to keep searching for hidden areas that may reward you with extra ammo or weapons. 
The two sequels – Marathon 2 and Marathon Infinity – are also available, although you’ll need to download the open-source files from Aleph One’s own website, or wait for them to arrive on Steam for a more straightforward download and installation process.

Perhaps the biggest game release of 2022 on the Mac, Total War: Warhammer III provided a truly epic conclusion to this popular series of strategy games. There’s no need to worry if you haven’t played any of the earlier games, though, as this three-quel includes an optional prologue, called The Lost God, that can act as an introduction for people who are new to the world of Warhammer.
This prologue explains that the great Beard God, Ursun, who is worshipped by the human kingdom of Kislev has been imprisoned in the demonic Realms Of Chaos. In Ursun’s absence, a terrible winter has fallen over Kislev, so you start by playing Prince Barkov of Kislev, who leads a small band of warriors to discover the fate of Ursun. This section also acts as a tutorial for people who might be new to strategy games, and when you’re up to speed you can progress to the main campaign in which rival factions compete to reach Ursun and use his godly powers for their own ends. 
As well the people of Kislev, you can command another human kingdom called Grand Cathay, or turn to the dark side by playing one of the many demonic princes who all have their own monstrous armies. There’s Nurgle, the Plague Lord, whose somewhat squishy troops spread disease and decay, along with Khorne, the Blood God, the hedonistic Slaanesh, and Tzeentch, the master of Chaos Magic. And, finally, there’s the uber Daemon Price, whose powers – and even body parts – can be customized so that you can create a playing style that’s all your own. You can also buy additional DLC packs that add new factions and races to the game. There’s also a free add-on called Immortal Empires, which brings together campaign maps, factions and battles from all three Warhammer games into one vast and endlessly replayable series of battles.
The good news is that the game will run on any Mac with an M1 or M2 processor – and we found that it ran at a smooth 30-40fps at 1920×1080 resolution even on a 24-inch iMac with a standard M1 processor. But while Intel Macs with AMD graphics may be able to run the game, there are a few technical glitches that can affect these Macs, so the game isn’t ‘officially supported’ on Intel Macs.

There aren’t a lot of sports games available on the Mac, but the Football Manager series is a longtime supporter, and we get the 2024 edition at the same time as the PC and console versions too. There’s also a new version of Football Manager 2024 Touch available for the iPhone, iPad and Apple TV. And, somewhat confusingly, the App Store also has a separate version, called Football Manager Mobile, which is only available to Netflix subscribers.
One of the biggest changes is the arrival of the ‘J-League’, with 60 Japanese teams now added to the game, along with Japanese language support as well. There are also new playing modes, such as ‘Real World’ where players in your games move to new teams on the same dates as they do in real life.
Each new version of the game tends to bring graphical improvements, and FM24 provides smoother animations for players as they charge around the pitch, more realistic physics for ball movement, and enhanced lighting effects to create a greater sense of atmosphere. And, of course, there are the inevitable AI features, such as the introduction of ‘Intermediaries’ that you can hire to go out and hustle for the best prices when you’re thinking of selling some players. There are also new Set Piece Coaches, who can help you to choose the best players for events such as free-kicks and corners. However, you’re up against tougher AI managers on opposition teams too, as they can now make smarter decisions when purchasing players that suit their tactical style.
The game also follows recent trends in tactical play, such as the greater use of positional play, which allows players to switch positions when your team has possession. The sheer depth of all these tactical options means that Football Manager can be a bit daunting for more casual fans of the game, but there’s a demo version available on both Steam and Epic, so you can have a quick kick-about to see how you get on before buying the full game.

It’s been quite a while since any of the Grid games were released on the Mac and, in fact, the Windows version of Grid Legends was first launched back at the start of 2022. However, the Deluxe Edition that’s launched on the Mac App Store does include all the game’s recent DLC add-ons – listed at more than $60/£60 on Steam for the Windows version – so it’s great value for racing fans on the Mac.
You don’t have to be an ace F1 driver to play Grid Legends, though, as the game includes a variety of different modes that can appeal to casual players as well as experienced drivers who want a more demanding and realistic driving simulation. The game starts by throwing you into its Story mode, called Driven To Glory, which follows the Seneca Racing team as it tries to make its name in the new season. As well as following the action through a series of races, the Story mode is also presented as a kind of behind-the-scenes documentary, with video cut-scenes and interviews with some of the main drivers (including an appearance by the pre-Doctor Who Ncuti Gatwa).
Story mode is a good way for beginners to get started, but more experienced drivers can jump straight ahead into the Career mode. This provides five difficulty levels, and allows you to work your way up from rookie to a seasoned pro driver. There are 10 different racing disciplines available, including Drift, Elimination and the arcade-action of Classic Car-nage, and the game lets you play on 24 different tracks in locations such as Brands Hatch, Barcelona Dubai and Miami.
As you progress through the season, you can unlock 120 different vehicles, with different handling properties to suit your driving style. There’s also a Garage mode where you can upgrade and fine-tune your car to suit different terrain and weather conditions. The game also includes a Race Creator mode, where you can design your own custom race events, using different tracks, vehicles and weather conditions. It’s a shame, though, that the Mac version of the game is single-player only, and doesn’t have the multiplayer mode that’s available on the PC version. The game also requires an Apple Silicon processor, and doesn’t run on older Intel Macs. However, it ran more than fast enough for my somewhat chaotic driving skills on an M1 iMac with medium graphics and 1600×900 resolution, so you don’t need a super-fast Mac to put your pedal to the metal.

There aren’t many ‘soulsborne’ games available on the Mac – so called because they follow the format of the popular Lost Souls and Bloodborne games available on PC and consoles – but Lies Of P arrived on the Mac App Store recently and immediately walked off with Apple’s award for Mac Game Of The Year.
The game is dedicated to Carlo Collodi, the author who created Pinocchio, and your main character is referred to as ‘the puppet of Gepetto’, so it’s clear who you’re supposed to be. This isn’t the cute Disney version of Pinocchio, though – for starters the little wooden boy has grown a bionic metal arm to give him some extra muscle, and one of your first tasks is to pick up a sword and choose a ‘path’ that determines your fighting style. The Path Of The Sweeper tends to focus on heavy, two-handed weapons, while the Path Of The Bastard lets you fight with lighter, faster weapons. Or, as a safe bet, you can choose the Path Of The Cricket, which combines elements of the other two fighting styles.
Your puppet boy wakes in the city of Krat, a kind of steam-punk dystopia that has been over-run by rampaging puppets who have turned against their human masters. Guided by a cricket called Gemini (because Disney owns the name ‘Jiminy Cricket’) you fight your way across the city to locate Gepetto and end the puppet revolt. Like all soulsborne games, Lies Of P is very challenging, with a wide range of combat moves and skills that you have to master as you fight your way across the city. And, as the name suggests, the game also allows you to choose between telling lies or the truth as you encounter other characters in the game. The developers recommend using a game controller, rather than mouse and keyboard, and the game only runs on Apple Silicon, with no support for older Intel Macs. An M2 is recommended, but we still found the game playable on an iMac with a basic M1 processor, when running on medium graphics settings at 1920×1080, so most recent Mac models should be able to handle the game without too much trouble.
Which Mac do I need to play modern games well?
Macs have evolved into capable gaming machines, particularly with the transition to Apple Silicon, though they still face significant performance and value gaps compared to dedicated Windows gaming PCs. While Apple’s latest hardware can run demanding AAA titles, the experience often requires high-end configurations to match the fluidity found on other platforms.
Here’s a selection of games and their Mac hardware requirements. 

GameHardware requirementsPerformance Notes

Cyberpunk 2077M4 Pro Mac mini (14/20 core)~63 fps at 1440p (High settings, no Ray Tracing).
InzoiM2/M3 MacBook Pro60–90 fps at 1080p/1440p (High/Very High settings).
Civilization VIIM2 Pro MacBook Pro~55 fps at 1440p (High settings).
Resident Evil 3M2 Pro MacBook ProSmooth performance at native resolutions 
Elder Scrolls OnlineM2 Pro MacBook Pro~40 fps at 1440p (High settings) via Rosetta.





What is the best way to run a PC game on a Mac
The best way to run a PC game on a Mac depends on the game itself and your hardware, but the options generally fall into three categories: native Mac ports, compatibility layers, and virtual machines. Here’s a breakdown of the most effective approaches.
Native Mac Ports: The simplest and most reliable way to play a PC game on a Mac is to choose titles that have been natively ported to macOS. All the games we have reviewed above run natively on macOS. This avoids the performance penalties of emulation or translation layers. 
Many major titles now ship with native Apple Silicon support, including Cyberpunk 2077 Ultimate Edition, Civilization VII, Frostpunk 2, and Assassin’s Creed Shadows.
Key consideration: Native ports are the best option when available, but the library is still smaller than Windows. Most native Mac games require Apple Silicon (M1 or newer) and at least 16GB of RAM for demanding titles. 
Compatibility Layers (CrossOver / Game Porting Toolkit): For Windows-only games that lack a Mac port, compatibility layers are the next best option. CodeWeavers CrossOver is the leading commercial solution. As described in our Best Virtual Machine Software for Mac guide, CrossOver translates Windows API calls into macOS equivalents, allowing many Windows apps and games to run natively rather than through a virtual machine. CrossOver offers a polished consumer-friendly interface with regular updates that improve compatibility with popular titles like Diablo IV and Path of Exile 2. It doesn’t require a Windows license, making it lighter and more affordable than a full VM.
Key consideration: Compatibility is still the biggest limitation – not every Windows game works, and performance can vary. 
Virtual Machines (Parallels Desktop, VMware Fusion): Virtual machines let you run a full copy of Windows alongside macOS, which can be useful for games that don’t work through compatibility layers. However, this approach carries a significant performance overhead because the game is running through both a hypervisor and the Windows emulation layer. That’s why CrossOver is generally preferred for gaming because it avoids the overhead of a full VM.
Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion are the top VM options, but they require a Windows license and are best suited for older or less demanding games. 
Key consideration: VMs are generally the slowest option for gaming and should be considered a last resort for demanding titles.
Which Macs are best for gaming? 
While it will be hard to replicate the gaming performance of a gaming PC without spending a lot more, and especially hard to get the equivalent gaming performance of a PlayStation 5 or similar, we consider the following Macs to be best for gaming. 
Note, you will require an Apple Silicon Mac. Intel Macs, by contrast, struggle with newer releases and are increasingly unsupported.

 FAQ 


1.
How Apple has made Macs better for gaming
Apple has introduced several software features to bridge the performance gap. Here are some of the technologies designed to maximize hardware efficiency. 
MetalFX Frame Interpolation & Denoising: Part of the Metal 4 API, these features use AI to generate extra frames and improve lighting effects like real-time path tracing.
Game Mode: This feature prioritizes gaming tasks on the CPU and GPU while reducing latency for wireless controllers and AirPods.
Game Porting Toolkit 2: This free set of tools created by Apple helps developers bring Windows games to Mac faster, supporting advanced features like Ray Tracing on M3 and M4 chips
Dedicated Games App: macOS Tahoe introduces a centralized hub for tracking achievements, friends, and launching titles from the App Store or Apple Arcade.





2.
Do these games run natively on macOS, or do they require emulation?
All of the games included in this list run natively on macOS. We’ve avoided titles that rely primarily on emulation or compatibility layers because that often leads to performance issues and inconsistent long-term support.





3.
What’s the minimum Mac I need to play these games?
The games on this list require M1 Mac or newer. More demanding titles benefit from 16GB of RAM and a Pro or Max chip, but many will still run well on base-model MacBooks with adjusted settings.





4.
Are Mac versions missing features compared to Windows versions?
Unfortunately it is a fact that some ports lag behind Windows in updates or mod support, but for most players the core experience is the same. We call out meaningful differences in our reviews when they affect gameplay or value.





5.
Is it better to buy games on Steam or the Mac App Store?
Steam may offer incentives, such as sales prices and easier access to updates and mods. The Mac App Store is convenient and tightly integrated with macOS, but it can be more expensive and slower to receive updates.





6.
Do these games support controllers on Mac?
Many do. PlayStation and Xbox controllers work well on macOS, though some games still play best with keyboard and mouse. We note controller support in individual game entries where it matters.





7.
Will these games work on future versions of macOS?
Games with active developer support are far more likely to remain compatible with future macOS updates. 





8.
Do I need to change settings to get good performance?
Often, yes. Even on Apple silicon Macs, lowering resolution or graphics settings can significantly improve frame rates. Most of the games here offer flexible options that let you balance visuals and performance.





9.
Is the MacBook Airs good enough for gaming?
Surprisingly, yes, but within limits. Base-model MacBook Airs can handle many of these games well, especially turn-based and indie titles. Sustained performance may drop during long sessions due to passive cooling, but casual and moderate gaming is very feasible.





10.
Why aren’t more big AAA games on Mac?
Game development is still heavily centered on Windows and consoles, and macOS remains a smaller market. That’s slowly changing as Apple silicon matures, but Mac gaming still relies on selective ports rather than simultaneous releases.





11.
Can I use Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit to play games on my Mac? 
The Game Porting Toolkit isn’t a consumer product, but some Mac enthusiasts have discovered that it can also be used to run many Windows games directly on macOS. However, tools like CrossOver are a much easier to use solution for playing PC games on a Mac. For games developers the GPTK is a useful tool for optimizing Windows games for the Mac. 





That’s it! We’re done. But if you want to read even more about your software options, why don’t you check out our guide to the

title: Ted Lasso is here to shake up Apple’s quiet August–but big things are on the way
content:
Macworld


Ever since Apple pulled out of Macworld New York back in 2023, August is traditionally a pretty slow month for Apple releases, but it’s a big one for the Apple rumor mill.
We don’t expect any new hardware this month with the looming iPhone/Apple Watch event coming in September. If you like your surprises spoiled, though, August is a good month for Apple rumors. Production will kick up for the new iPhones and Apple Watches, and sometimes other hardware that Apple plans to release in the fall. And with large-scale manufacturing comes leaks. 
So August will probably be the month we get our best picture of the upcoming iPhones, Macs, and other devices Apple has planned for release this fall. Plus, the new operating systems are well into their public beta testing process—those will continue, but there probably won’t be any big surprises.
This will be Tim Cook’s last month as CEO, as John Ternus will take over the role on September 1. Oh, and Ted Lasso is back!
OS 27 beta testing continues
We don’t expect any new hardware in August (not with the big September iPhone event so close), but there will be plenty of software to check out if you participate in the beta program.
We’re currently at the fourth beta release for all the OS 27 updates: iOS, macOS, iPadOS, watchOS, visionOS. New releases go out to developers every two weeks or so, with the public beta testers getting the same builds a day or two later. So expect two more beta releases in August, potentially three.
At this point, most of the big features and changes in the OS 27 betas are already here, and Apple is just refining things, fixing bugs, and optimizing performance. We’ll be scouring the builds for potential hidden information about the upcoming products, too.
Services
Apple TV+
Here are the shows, series, and movies we expect to release on Apple TV+ in August. If you want to know what’s coming later, check our full guide to upcoming Apple TV+ content.
Ted Lasso (season 4): Apple’s big breakout hit show returns after a three-year hiatus. August 5

Apple releases most Apple Arcade games on the first Friday of each month. Check our Apple Arcade FAQ for a full list of Apple Arcade games and more details on the service. title: Apple Launches New Legal Challenge Against UK Backdoor Demand
content:
Apple last month filed a new legal complaint with the UK's Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) over the British government's demand for access to encrypted iCloud backups belonging to UK users, according to an order issued by the court and reported by the Financial Times.


The Home Office previously agreed to drop its original demand for a backdoor covering UK and U.S. customers alike, after a diplomatic row with Washington. The British government subsequently issued a new technical capability notice (TCN) to Apple last year, limited to users in the UK.

Technical capability notices are issued under the UK's Investigatory Powers Act, which the government says is necessary to investigate terrorism and child sexual abuse. They can force companies to hand UK security services access to customer data, even when that data is encrypted.

separate complaint against such notices at the IPT, with that case due to be heard in December.

title: iPhone price hikes are coming: ‘Absolutely no doubt’
content:
Macworld


When Apple hiked prices last month, one notable product that was spared from the sticker shock was the iPhone. All seven of the iPhone models Apple currently sells, including the two-year-old iPhone 16 and 16 Plus, have the same starting prices as before: $599 for the iPhone 17e, increasing incrementally all the way up to the $1,199 Phone 17 Pro Max.
In just a few weeks, that’s likely to change. After hearing reports for months that the iPhone 18 Pro will come with a price hike this fall, Mark Gurman weighs in with a comment in his latest Power On Newsletter. In no uncertain terms, he says prices will be going up on iPhones this fall. The only question is, how much.
In a response to a reader question about iPhone prices, Gurman says in plain language: “There is absolutely no doubt that Apple will raise iPhone prices, for a variety of reasons.” Chief among them, of course, is the current memory supply crunch that has affected the entire industry and is largely responsible for Apple’s recent Mac and iPad price hikes. But Gurman also says the new camera system in the iPhone 18 Pro, which is expected to have a variable-aperture lens, is also pricier than the current model.
It’s notable that the price of Apple’s high-end iPhone hasn’t really changed much over the past decade. When Apple introduced the iPhone X in 2017 with a $999 price tag, it set a new standard for flagship phones. However, the iPhone 17 Pro, which is most comparable to that model, costs just $100 more, starting at $1,099. Granted, the larger iPhone 17 Pro Max pushes it even higher, with storage options all the way up to $1,999, but iPhone prices have remained remarkably stable for a while, even with bigger screens, more and better cameras, and higher-end components.
As far as the extent of the hikes, Gurman is somewhat unclear, though he says “the iPad and Mac increases in recent weeks have given us a bit of a road map.” Therefore, he expects $100-$200 price increases, and a starting price for the folding iPhone Ultra of “at least $2,000, if not more.” Less clear is whether Apple will adjust the prices of the standard iPhone 17 and 17e, which aren’t expected to get updates until next spring.

content:
